The Kansas Forestry, Fish and Game Commission says, "The intent of the Act is to clearly prohibit the taking of endangered species. There is no emphasis on research programs necessary to perpetuate endangered species."
There is no question that protection is predominant in the text of the proposed legislation because laws providing that protection, as one aspect of management, must be uniform over the range of the endangered species in question. Rules that vary from State to State can be more easily evaded and animals that are as unique as endangered species might well be more apt to encourage abrogation of those variable rules than the more common species of wildlife.
Habitat management, as a matter of fact, is not deemphasized by an emphasis on protection. Provisions are made for management by various Federal land-managing agencies. There is no question that close Federal-State cooperation will be required to achieve levels of management needed. This will be accomplished through cooperative agreements in the form of recovery plans carried out within the authority of the proposed legislation.
Sole Jurisdiction. Section 2(d)(5) defines "Secretary" as the Secretary of the Interior or the Secretary of Commerce as program responsibilities are vested pursuant to the provisions of Reorganization Plan Numbered 4 of 1970. Thereby, jurisdiction for determining which of various groups of species are endangered is divided between the Secretary of the Interior and the Secretary of Commerce depending upon those jurisdictions so designated in Reorganization Plan Number 4. Kentucky and Florida indicated that they prefer that the Secretary of the Interior retain sole jurisdiction for making such determination.
